title: Tibet, 1950–1959
hookLine: Chinese forces entered Tibet; the Dalai Lama left for India, and others followed him into exile

cards: What would you carry if you had to leave home at night, on foot, over mountains, not knowing when you'd come back? A coat. Water.

A photograph, maybe. Some Tibetan families who crossed into India and Nepal speak of carrying something else too: a text wrapped in cloth, a small image of the Buddha, prayer beads, a teacher walking a few steps ahead.
Today isn't one night. It's a long exile, and the practice that went with it.

teach.b: In the years named in today's title, Chinese forces entered Tibet, and Tibet came under the government in Beijing.
The Chinese government and Tibetans in exile tell those years very differently, and this lesson won't settle that argument. What it can tell is what happened to a community of practice.

teach.h: THE DALAI LAMA LEAVES FOR INDIA.
teach.b: After unrest in Lhasa, the Dalai Lama, whom Tibetan Buddhists hold as a great teacher, left for India. Monks, nuns and lay families followed through the high passes.

In India, with very little, they rebuilt. Monasteries with the old names rose again, so a monastery from Tibet might now stand in the hot plains of southern India. Schools taught children their language and their texts.
Debate courtyards filled again with monks clapping as they argued a point, just as their teachers had.
And in his public teaching from exile, the Dalai Lama has returned again and again to compassion, even for those he disagrees with. An opponent, he has said, can be your teacher of patience.
The Pali word is khanti, and the Dhammapada sets it very high.
In Max Müller's translation: "The Awakened call patience the highest penance." Patience here doesn't mean pretending nothing happened. Exile still hurts; homes are still missed.
Patience lets a person keep the grief without letting it harden into hate, and keep teaching while they wait.

how: Tibetan Buddhists in exile keep their practice in rebuilt monasteries, schools and community centers, and some hold Tibet and all who suffered in their daily prayers and loving-kindness practice.

practice: Hold refugees in metta, loving-kindness: bring to mind anyone who has had to leave home, Tibetan families, refugees from anywhere, someone you know, and with each out-breath send a simple wish in words that feel true, may you be safe, may you find a home.
If the mind drifts to the news or to blame, come back to the wish. Last, widen it to everyone caught up in that history, on every side.

wordCard.voice: Tibet. The high land whose teachers and families carried their practice into exile, and rebuilt it, monastery by monastery, far from home. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali khanti: patience, forbearance; the virtue the Dalai Lama says an opponent can teach.

carryVoice: Your line: the long exile. Grief kept, and the teaching kept, while they wait. Rest well.
